analysis.title: Is the case for commodities still intact?
key_insights: Brent crude has slipped to near USD 91.45/bbl, down from as high as USD 118/bbl at end October, as markets price a greater chance of Middle East de-escalation and recovering supply.
A stronger-than-expected 'Blue Wave' US midterms outcome has encouraged markets to price in more US-Iran de-escalation.
Middle Eastern loadings have recovered substantially from earlier disruption, and softer demand expectations have also weighed on oil prices.

Lower oil prices do not remove supply constraints. Higher insurance and freight costs have raised the delivered cost of crude, and fragile shipping flows and low inventories leave energy markets vulnerable.
Global visible oil inventories stood at 7.8 billion barrels at end September, more than 500 million barrels below February levels.
Copper is susceptible to AI jitters but faces constrained supply and long-term demand from power grids, data centers and electrification. UBS prefers copper.

Gold fell more than 9% in the week ending 20 November to a 14-month low near USD 3,500/oz, its worst weekly decline since late March. UBS still sees central bank buying, robust Chinese demand and public debt concerns as a backstop despite high real yields and a firmer USD.
Investment view is to favor broad, actively managed commodity exposure with a preference for copper and strategic gold holdings, sized for price volatility.
From January 1999 through May 2026 commodities had a 0.44 correlation with global equities and -0.04 with US bonds, supporting diversification.
Leadership can rotate rapidly across energy, metals, agriculture and gold, so UBS suggests diversified, regularly rebalanced exposure while noting volatility and holding-cost risks.
